desc.CIS 12.6: Use of Secure Network Management and Communication Protocols — [IG2] Use secure network management and communication protocols, such as 802.1X, Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2) Enterprise or greater.
desc.CIS 12.7: Ensure Remote Devices Utilise a VPN and Are Connecting to an Enterprise's AAA Infrastructure — [IG2] Require users to authenticate to enterprise-managed VPN and authentication infrastructure prior to accessing enterprise resources on end-user devices.
desc.CIS 12.8: Establish and Maintain Dedicated Computing Resources for All Administrative Work — [IG3] Establish and maintain dedicated computing resources, either physically or logically separated, for all administrative tasks or tasks requiring administrative access. The computing resources should be segmented from the enterprise's primary network and not be allowed internet access.
desc.CIS 13: Network Monitoring and Defence — Operate processes and tooling to establish and maintain comprehensive network monitoring and defence against security threats across the enterprise's network infrastructure and user base.
desc.CIS 13.1: Centralise Security Event Alerting — [IG2] Centralise security event alerting across enterprise assets for log correlation and analysis. Best practice implementation requires the use of a SIEM.
desc.CIS 13.2: Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Detection Solution — [IG2] Deploy a host-based intrusion detection solution on enterprise assets, where supported.
desc.CIS 13.3: Deploy a Network Intrusion Detection Solution — [IG2] Deploy a network intrusion detection solution on enterprise assets, where supported. Example implementations include the use of a network intrusion detection system (NIDS) or equivalent cloud service provider capabilities.
desc.CIS 13.4: Perform Traffic Filtering Between Network Segments — [IG1] Perform traffic filtering between network segments, where such filtering is technically supported.
desc.CIS 13.5: Manage Access Control for Remote Assets — [IG2] Manage access control for assets remotely connecting to enterprise resources. The authentication solution must incorporate MFA, where supported.
desc.CIS 13.6: Collect Network Traffic Flow Logs — [IG2] Collect network traffic flow logs and/or network traffic to review and alert upon from network devices.
desc.CIS 13.7: Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Prevention Solution — [IG3] Deploy a host-based intrusion prevention solution on enterprise assets, where supported. Example implementations include the use of an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) client.
desc.CIS 13.8: Deploy a Network Intrusion Prevention Solution — [IG3] Deploy a network intrusion prevention solution, where appropriate. Example implementations include the use of a Network Intrusion Prevention System (NIPS) or equivalent cloud service provider capabilities.
desc.CIS 13.9: Deploy Port-Level Access Control — [IG3] Deploy port-level access control. 802.1X and/or MAC address-based controls may be used to ensure that only authorised systems can connect to a network.
desc.CIS 13.10: Perform Application Layer Filtering — [IG3] Perform application layer filtering. Example implementations include a filtering proxy or a next-generation firewall.
desc.CIS 13.11: Tune Security Event Alerting Thresholds — [IG3] Tune security event alerting thresholds monthly, or more frequently.
desc.CIS 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training — Establish and maintain a security awareness programme to influence behaviour among the workforce to be security conscious and to equip them with the skills to reduce cybersecurity risks.
desc.CIS 14.1: Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness Programme — [IG1] Establish and maintain a security awareness programme. The purpose of a security awareness programme is to educate the enterprise's workforce on how to interact with enterprise assets and data in a secure manner. Review and update content annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 14.2: Train Workforce Members to Recognise Social Engineering Attacks — [IG1] Train workforce members to recognise social engineering attacks, such as phishing, pre-texting, and tailgating.
desc.CIS 14.3: Train Workforce Members on Authentication Best Practices — [IG1] Train workforce members on authentication best practices. Example topics include MFA, password composition, and credential management.
desc.CIS 14.4: Train Workforce on Data Handling Best Practices — [IG1] Train workforce members on how to identify and properly store, transfer, archive, and destroy sensitive data. This also includes training workforce members on clear screen and desk policies.
desc.CIS 14.5: Train Workforce Members on Causes of Unintentional Data Exposure — [IG1] Train workforce members to be aware of causes for unintentional data exposure. Example topics include mis-delivery of sensitive data, losing a portable end-user device, or publishing data to unintended audiences.
desc.CIS 14.6: Train Workforce Members on Recognising and Reporting Security Incidents — [IG1] Train workforce members to be able to recognise a potential incident and be able to report such an incident.
desc.CIS 14.7: Train Workforce on How to Identify and Report if Their Enterprise Assets are Missing Security Updates — [IG2] Train workforce to understand how to verify and report out-of-date software patches or any failures in automated processes and tools. Part of this training should include notifying IT personnel of any failures in automated processes and tools.
desc.CIS 14.8: Train Workforce on the Dangers Associated with Connecting to and Transmitting Data Over Insecure Networks — [IG2] Train workforce members on the dangers of connecting to and transmitting data over insecure networks for enterprise activities. If the enterprise has remote workers, training must include guidance to ensure all work-related activities including the use of enterprise assets and data, are done over enterprise-managed VPN.
desc.CIS 14.9: Conduct Role-Specific Security Awareness and Skills Training — [IG2] Conduct role-specific security awareness and skills training. Example implementations include secure system administration courses for IT professionals, OWASP Top 10 vulnerability awareness and prevention training for web application developers, and phishing and other social engineering awareness training for end users.
desc.CIS 15: Service Provider Management — Develop a process to evaluate service providers who hold sensitive data or are responsible for an enterprise's critical IT platforms or processes, ensuring these providers are protecting those platforms and data appropriately.
desc.CIS 15.1: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Providers — [IG2] Establish and maintain an inventory of service providers. The inventory is to list all known service providers, include classification(s), and designate an enterprise contact for each service provider. Review and update the inventory annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 15.2: Establish and Maintain a Service Provider Management Policy — [IG2] Establish and maintain a service provider management policy. Ensure the policy addresses the classification, inventory, assessment, monitoring, and decommissioning of service providers. Review and update the policy annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 15.3: Classify Service Providers — [IG2] Classify service providers. Classification considerations may include one or more characteristics, such as data sensitivity, data volume, availability requirements, applicable regulations, inherent risk, and mitigated risk. Update and review classifications annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 15.4: Ensure Service Provider Contracts Include Security Requirements — [IG2] Ensure service provider contracts include security requirements. Example requirements may include minimum security programme requirements, security incident and/or data breach notification and response requirements, data encryption requirements, and data disposal requirements.
desc.CIS 15.5: Assess Service Providers — [IG2] Assess service providers consistent with the enterprise's service provider management policy. Assessment scope may vary based on classification(s), and may include review of standardised assessment reports, such as Service Organisation Control 2 (SOC 2) and Payment Card Industry (PCI) Attestation of Compliance (AoC) reports, customised questionnaires, or other appropriately structured assessments.
desc.CIS 15.6: Monitor Service Providers — [IG2] Monitor service providers consistent with the enterprise's service provider management policy. Monitoring may include periodic reassessment of service provider classifications, reviewing service provider security programme effectiveness, and monitoring for breaches.
desc.CIS 15.7: Securely Decommission Service Providers — [IG2] Securely decommission service providers. Example considerations include service transition or termination agreement(s), including ensuring the security of data.
desc.CIS 16: Application Software Security — Manage the security life cycle of in-house developed, hosted, or acquired software in order to prevent, detect, and remediate security weaknesses before they can impact the enterprise.
desc.CIS 16.1: Establish and Maintain a Secure Application Development Process — [IG2] Establish and maintain a secure application development process. In the process, address such items as: secure application design standards, secure coding practices, developer training, vulnerability management, security of third-party code, and security testing methodologies. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 16.2: Establish and Maintain a Process to Accept and Address Software Vulnerabilities — [IG2] Establish and maintain a process to accept and address reports of software vulnerabilities, including providing a means for external parties to report. The process is to include such items as: a vulnerability tracking system, a process for intake of vulnerability reports, acceptance of reports, validation, remediation, and end-user notification.
desc.CIS 16.3: Perform Root Cause Analysis on Security Vulnerabilities — [IG2] Perform root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities. When reviewing vulnerabilities, root cause analysis should be used to identify and remediate the underlying cause.
desc.CIS 16.4: Establish and Manage an Inventory of Third-Party Software Components — [IG2] Establish and manage an updated inventory of third-party components used in development, often referred to as a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and components that are in Production. Monitor sources such as vendor advisories and the National Vulnerability Database to stay current on vulnerabilities and available updates for these components.
desc.CIS 16.5: Use Up-to-Date and Trusted Third-Party Software Components — [IG2] Use up-to-date and trusted third-party software components. When possible, choose established and maintained frameworks and libraries that provide adequate security. Acquire these components from trusted sources, validate their integrity, and keep them current.
desc.CIS 16.6: Establish and Maintain a Severity Rating System and Process for Application Vulnerabilities — [IG2] Establish and maintain a severity rating system and process for application vulnerabilities that facilitates prioritising the order in which discovered vulnerabilities are patched. The process includes rating sensitivities of the affected data and a risk weighting of the vulnerability. Vulnerabilities should be rated on a scale of 1-10 with 10 being the most severe risk for the enterprise. The rating system must factor in the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of the affected data.
desc.CIS 16.7: Use Standard Hardening Configuration Templates for Application Infrastructure — [IG2] Use standard, industry-recommended hardening configuration templates for application infrastructure components. This includes underlying servers, databases, and web servers, and applies to cloud containers, security groups, and other infrastructure components.
desc.CIS 16.8: Separate Production and Non-Production Systems — [IG2] Do not run non-production systems on production infrastructure.
desc.CIS 16.9: Train Developers in Application Security Concepts and Secure Coding — [IG2] Ensure that all software development personnel receive training in writing secure code for their specific development environment and responsibilities. Training can include general security principles and application security standard practices such as OWASP Top 10.
desc.CIS 16.10: Apply Secure Design Principles in Application Architectures — [IG2] Apply secure design principles in application architectures. Example principles include the following: least privilege and separation of duties, fail securely, complete mediation, economy of mechanism (keep it simple), full documentation, minimising attack surface area, avoiding security through obscurity.
desc.CIS 16.11: Leverage Vetted Modules or Services for Application Security Components — [IG2] Leverage vetted modules or services for application security components, such as identity management, encryption, and auditing and logging. Using platform features in critical security functions will reduce developer workload and minimise the likelihood of design or implementation errors.
desc.CIS 16.12: Implement Code-Level Security Checks — [IG3] Apply static code analysis tools to verify that coding practices meet defined security standards.
desc.CIS 16.13: Conduct Application Penetration Testing — [IG3] Conduct application penetration testing. For critical applications, authenticated penetration testing is preferred. Penetration testing must include, at a minimum, OWASP Top 10 issues.
desc.CIS 16.14: Conduct Threat Modelling — [IG2] Conduct threat modelling. For each of the enterprise's highest risk applications, conduct threat modelling to identify attacker goals, attack surfaces, attack techniques, mitigations, and residual risk.
desc.CIS 17: Incident Response Management — Establish a programme to develop and maintain an incident response capability in order to prepare, detect, contain, and recover from attacks.
desc.CIS 17.1: Designate Personnel to Manage Incident Handling — [IG1] Designate one key person, and at least one backup, who will manage the enterprise's incident handling process. Management personnel are responsible for the coordination and documentation of incident response and recovery efforts and can consist of one or more individuals from the enterprise.
desc.CIS 17.2: Establish and Maintain Contact Information for Reporting Security Incidents — [IG1] Establish and maintain contact information for parties that need to be informed of security incidents. Contacts to consider may include internal (e.g. the executive team, HR, communications and accounting departments) and external contacts (e.g. law enforcement, cyber insurance provider, relevant government agencies, vendors, public relations firms).
desc.CIS 17.3: Establish and Maintain an Enterprise Process for Reporting Incidents — [IG1] Establish and maintain an enterprise process for the workforce to report security incidents. The process includes reporting timeframe, personnel to report to, mechanism for reporting, and the minimum information to be reported. Ensure the process is publicly available to all of the workforce.
desc.CIS 17.4: Establish and Maintain an Incident Response Process — [IG2] Establish and maintain an incident response process that addresses roles and responsibilities, compliance requirements, and a communication plan.
desc.CIS 17.5: Assign Key Roles and Responsibilities — [IG2] Assign key roles and responsibilities for incident response, including staff from legal, IT, information security, facilities, public relations, HR, incident responders, and analysts, as applicable. Review annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 17.6: Define Mechanisms for Communicating During Incident Response — [IG2] Determine which primary and secondary mechanisms will be used to communicate and report during a security incident. This includes what data can be shared and with whom, mechanisms for sharing data, and any legal or regulatory reporting requirements.
desc.CIS 17.7: Conduct Routine Incident Response Exercises — [IG2] Plan and conduct routine incident response exercises and scenarios for the workforce involved in the incident response to maintain awareness and comfort in responding to real-world threats. Exercises need to include both simulated and real-world scenarios.
desc.CIS 17.8: Conduct Post-Incident Reviews — [IG2] Conduct post-incident reviews. Post-incident reviews help prevent incident recurrence through identifying lessons learned and follow-up action.
desc.CIS 17.9: Establish and Maintain Security Incident Thresholds — [IG2] Establish and maintain security incident thresholds, including, at a minimum, differentiating between an incident and an event, and definition of severity levels for incidents.
desc.CIS 18: Penetration Testing — Test the effectiveness and resiliency of enterprise assets through identifying and exploiting weaknesses in controls (people, processes, and technology), and simulating the objectives and actions of an attacker.
desc.CIS 18.1: Establish and Maintain a Penetration Testing Programme — [IG2] Establish and maintain a penetration testing programme appropriate to the size, complexity, and maturity of the enterprise. A penetration testing programme includes such components as clear goals, defined scope, limitations, testing methodology, remediation, and exception processes. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur.
desc.CIS 18.2: Perform Periodic External Penetration Tests — [IG2] Perform periodic external penetration tests based on programme requirements, no less than annually. External penetration testing must include enterprise and environmental reconnaissance to detect exploitable information. Penetration testing requires specialised skills and experience and must be conducted through a qualified party.
desc.CIS 18.3: Remediate Penetration Test Findings — [IG2] Remediate penetration test findings based on the enterprise's policy for remediation scope and prioritisation.
desc.CIS 18.4: Validate Security Measures — [IG3] Validate security measures after each penetration test. If deemed necessary, modify rulesets and capabilities to detect the techniques used during testing.
desc.CIS 18.5: Perform Periodic Internal Penetration Tests — [IG3] Perform periodic internal penetration tests based on programme requirements, no less than annually. The scope of internal penetration testing includes, at a minimum, the enterprise's intranet and internal systems.

about.title: CIS Controls v8
about.blurb: The CIS Controls are a prioritised set of 18 safeguard categories and 153 individual safeguards designed to defend against the most prevalent cyber attacks. Controls are organised into three Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3) based on organisational risk profile and resources.

p: IG1 (Basic): 56 safeguards for small organisations with limited IT/security expertise. Represent essential cyber hygiene.
IG2 (Foundational): adds 74 safeguards for organisations with moderate IT complexity and regulatory obligations.
IG3 (Advanced): adds 23 safeguards for mature organisations with significant security teams and high-risk profiles.

Each Control group has a title, description, and a set of numbered Safeguards. Safeguard IDs follow the pattern CIS X.Y where X is the Control number and Y is the Safeguard number within that Control.

groups.name: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
groups.desc: Actively manage (inventory, track, and correct) all enterprise assets connected to the infrastructure — physically, virtually, remotely, and those within cloud environments — to accurately know the totality of assets that need to be monitored and protected.
achieved: A complete, up-to-date hardware asset inventory exists covering all connected devices.
Unauthorised devices are detected and addressed within a defined SLA.
Passive and active discovery tools run continuously or on a scheduled basis.
Asset ownership is assigned for every entry in the inventory.
evidence: CMDB or asset inventory export showing all physical and virtual assets with owner and classification
Network discovery scan reports (e.g. Nmap, Qualys, Rapid7) with timestamps
Alerts or tickets raised for unauthorised device detections

items.name: Establish and Maintain Detailed Enterprise Asset Inventory
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain an accurate, detailed, and up-to-date inventory of all enterprise assets with potential to store or process data, including end-user devices, network devices, non-computing/IoT devices, and servers. Ensure the inventory captures the network address, hardware address, machine name, data asset owner, department, and whether the asset has been approved to connect to the network.
achieved: Inventory contains hardware address, IP, hostname, owner, and department for every asset.
Inventory is reviewed and reconciled at least quarterly.
evidence: Asset inventory spreadsheet or CMDB extract
Quarterly reconciliation log

items.name: Address Unauthorised Assets
items.desc: [IG1] Ensure that a process exists to address unauthorised assets on a weekly basis. The enterprise may choose to remove the asset from the network, deny the asset from connecting remotely to the network, or quarantine the asset.
achieved: Documented process for handling unauthorised assets exists and is followed.
Evidence of unauthorised devices being quarantined or removed.
evidence: Incident or change tickets for unauthorised device handling
NAC quarantine logs

items.name: Utilise an Active Discovery Tool
items.desc: [IG2] Utilise an active discovery tool to identify assets connected to the enterprise's network. Configure the active discovery tool to execute daily, or more frequently.
achieved: Active scanning tool is deployed and runs on a defined schedule.
Scan results are reviewed and fed into the asset inventory.
evidence: Discovery tool configuration showing scan schedule
Scan output reports

items.name: Use Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Logging
items.desc: [IG2] Use DHCP logging on all DHCP servers or IP address management tools to update the enterprise's asset inventory. Review and use logs to update the asset inventory at a minimum weekly, or more frequently.
achieved: DHCP logs are retained and reviewed to validate and update asset records.
evidence: DHCP server log exports
Evidence of inventory updates driven by DHCP data

items.name: Use a Passive Asset Discovery Tool
items.desc: [IG3] Use a passive discovery tool to identify assets connected to the enterprise's network. Review and use scans to update the enterprise's asset inventory at a minimum weekly, or more frequently.
achieved: Passive discovery (e.g. network traffic analysis) supplements active scanning.
New assets appear in inventory within 24 hours of connection.
evidence: Passive discovery tool configuration and output reports

groups.name: Inventory and Control of Software Assets
groups.desc: Actively manage (inventory, track, and correct) all software on the network so that only authorised software is installed and can execute, and unauthorised and unmanaged software is found and prevented from installation or execution.
achieved: A complete software inventory exists covering all installed applications, SaaS subscriptions, and libraries.
Unauthorised software is detected and removed or blocked within a defined SLA.
Only software from the approved catalogue is permitted to run on managed devices.
Software inventory is reconciled against approved catalogue at least monthly.
evidence: Software asset inventory or SAM tool export
Approved software catalogue
Application whitelisting or endpoint policy configuration evidence

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Software Inventory
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a detailed inventory of all licensed software installed on enterprise assets. The software inventory must document the title, publisher, initial install/use date, and business purpose for each entry. Review and update the inventory bi-annually or more frequently.
achieved: Inventory lists all installed software with title, publisher, version, and business owner.
Inventory reviewed at least every six months.
evidence: Software inventory export from endpoint management or SAM tool

items.name: Ensure Authorised Software is Currently Supported
items.desc: [IG1] Ensure that only currently supported software is designated as authorised in the software inventory. Unsupported software should be tagged as unsupported and reviewed monthly.
achieved: All authorised software has an active support/maintenance status.
EOL software is identified and remediation-tracked.
evidence: EOL software report from SAM or patch management tool

items.name: Address Unauthorised Software
items.desc: [IG1] Ensure that unauthorised software is either removed, quarantined, or the exception is documented with business justification.
achieved: Process for handling unauthorised software is defined and followed.

evidence: Tickets or change records for unauthorised software removal
Exception register

items.name: Utilise Automated Software Inventory Tools
items.desc: [IG2] Utilise software inventory tools, such as endpoint management or application management tools, throughout the enterprise to automate the collection of the software inventory.
achieved: Automated discovery tool covers all managed endpoints.
Inventory is updated automatically on a defined schedule.
evidence: Endpoint management tool configuration and coverage report

items.name: Allowlist Authorised Software
items.desc: [IG3] Use technical controls such as application allowlisting to ensure that only authorised software can execute on enterprise assets.
achieved: Application allowlisting policy is enforced on all managed endpoints.
Exceptions require formal approval.
evidence: Allowlisting tool configuration
Exception approval records

items.name: Allowlist Authorised Libraries
items.desc: [IG3] Use technical controls to ensure that only authorised software libraries, such as specific .dll, .ocx, .so, and other similar files, are allowed to load into a system process.
achieved: Library allowlisting or integrity monitoring is in place for critical systems.
evidence: File integrity monitoring (FIM) or allowlisting configuration for library paths

items.name: Allowlist Authorised Scripts
items.desc: [IG3] Use technical controls such as script allowlisting or code signing to ensure that only authorised scripts, such as specific .ps1, .py, and other similar files, are allowed to execute.
achieved: Script execution policy restricts unsigned or non-whitelisted scripts.
PowerShell and other scripting engines are configured to enforce policy.
evidence: Script execution policy configuration (e.g. PowerShell Constrained Language Mode settings)

groups.name: Data Protection
groups.desc: Develop processes and technical controls to identify, classify, securely handle, retain, and dispose of data.
achieved: A data classification scheme is defined and applied across all data stores.
Sensitive data is encrypted at rest and in transit.
Data retention and disposal procedures are implemented and enforced.
DLP controls monitor and prevent unauthorised data exfiltration.
evidence: Data classification policy and scheme documentation
Encryption configuration evidence for storage and transport (e.g. TLS, AES-256)
DLP policy configuration and incident reports
Data disposal records and certificates of destruction

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Data Management Process
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a data management process. In the process, address data sensitivity, data owner, handling of data, data retention limits, and disposal requirements, based on sensitivity and retention standards for the enterprise.
achieved: Data management process is documented, approved, and communicated.
Data owners are assigned for all sensitive data types.
evidence: Data management policy document
Data owner assignment register

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Data Inventory
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a data inventory based on the enterprise's data management process. Inventory sensitive data at a minimum. Review and update inventory annually, at a minimum, with a priority on sensitive data.
achieved: Data inventory covers all sensitive data stores with classification, location, and owner.
Inventory reviewed at least annually.
evidence: Data inventory register or data map

items.name: Configure Data Access Control Lists
items.desc: [IG1] Configure data access control lists based on a user's need to know. Apply data access control lists, also known as access permissions, to local and remote file systems, databases, and applications.
achieved: Access to sensitive data is restricted to those with documented business need.
Access control lists are reviewed at least quarterly.
evidence: Access control configuration screenshots or exports
Access review reports

items.name: Enforce Data Retention
items.desc: [IG1] Retain data according to the enterprise's data management process. Data retention must include both minimum and maximum timeframes.
achieved: Automated retention policies are configured in document management and email systems.
Retention schedules are aligned with legal and regulatory requirements.
evidence: Retention policy configuration in DMS or email platform
Retention schedule document

items.name: Securely Dispose of Data
items.desc: [IG1] Securely dispose of data as outlined in the enterprise's data management process. Ensure the disposal process and method are commensurate with the data sensitivity.
achieved: Secure disposal procedures are in place for all media types.
Certificates of destruction are retained for sensitive data disposal.
evidence: Certificates of destruction from approved disposal provider
Data disposal log

items.name: Encrypt Data on End-User Devices
items.desc: [IG1] Encrypt data on end-user devices containing sensitive data. Example implementations include BitLocker for Windows, FileVault for macOS, and full-disk encryption on mobile devices.
achieved: Full-disk encryption is enforced on all managed end-user devices.
Encryption status is monitored and non-compliant devices are remediated.
evidence: MDM/endpoint management encryption compliance report

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Data Classification Scheme
items.desc: [IG2] Establish and maintain an overall data classification scheme for the enterprise. Enterprises may use labels such as 'Sensitive', 'Confidential', and 'Public' and classify data according to those labels.
achieved: Classification scheme is documented with clear criteria for each level.
Staff are trained on how to classify data correctly.
evidence: Data classification policy
Training completion records

items.name: Document Data Flows
items.desc: [IG2] Document data flows. Data flow documentation includes service provider data flows and should be based on the enterprise's data management process.
achieved: Data flow diagrams cover all sensitive data movement including to/from third parties.
Data flows are reviewed when systems change.
evidence: Data flow diagrams
Third-party data transfer agreements

items.name: Encrypt Data on Removable Media
items.desc: [IG2] Encrypt data on removable media.
achieved: All removable media containing sensitive data is encrypted using approved algorithms.
Port control prevents use of unapproved removable media.
evidence: Removable media encryption policy
Port control configuration

items.name: Encrypt Sensitive Data in Transit
items.desc: [IG2] Encrypt sensitive data in transit. Example implementations include Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Open Secure Shell (OpenSSH).
achieved: TLS 1.2 or higher is enforced for all data in transit.
Unencrypted protocols are blocked for sensitive data paths.
evidence: TLS configuration reports
Network policy documentation blocking cleartext protocols

items.name: Encrypt Sensitive Data at Rest
items.desc: [IG2] Encrypt sensitive data at rest on servers, applications, and databases containing sensitive data.
achieved: Database and application-level encryption is enabled for all sensitive data stores.
Encryption keys are managed using a key management service.
evidence: Database encryption configuration
KMS key policy documentation

items.name: Segment Data Processing and Storage Based on Sensitivity
items.desc: [IG2] Segment data processing and storage based on the sensitivity of the data. Do not process sensitive data on enterprise assets intended for lower sensitivity data.
achieved: High-sensitivity data is processed only on designated, hardened systems.
Network segmentation separates sensitive data processing zones.
evidence: Network architecture diagram showing segmentation
System classification inventory

items.name: Deploy a Data Loss Prevention Solution
items.desc: [IG2] Implement an automated tool, such as a DLP solution, to identify all sensitive data stored, processed, or transmitted through enterprise assets, including those located on-site or at a remote service provider, and update the enterprise's data inventory.
achieved: DLP solution is deployed covering endpoints, email, and cloud channels.
DLP incidents are reviewed and acted upon within defined SLAs.
evidence: DLP tool configuration and coverage report
DLP incident response log

items.name: Log Sensitive Data Access
items.desc: [IG3] Log sensitive data access, including modification and disposal. Example implementations include logging access to all sensitive data stored in structured data repositories such as databases or data warehouses.
achieved: Audit logging is enabled for all access to sensitive data stores.
Logs are centralised, protected, and reviewed for anomalies.
evidence: Database audit log configuration
SIEM alert rules for sensitive data access

groups.name: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software
groups.desc: Establish and maintain the secure configuration of enterprise assets (end-user devices, network devices, non-computing/IoT devices, and servers) and software (operating systems and applications).
achieved: Security configuration baselines are defined for all asset and software types.
Baseline compliance is monitored continuously and deviations are remediated.
Default credentials and unnecessary services are removed from all assets.
Configuration changes go through a formal change management process.
evidence: CIS Benchmark or equivalent hardening baseline documents
Configuration compliance scan reports showing baseline adherence percentage
Change management records for configuration changes
Default account removal evidence

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a secure configuration process for enterprise assets and software. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.
achieved: Secure configuration process is documented, approved, and reviewed annually.
Process covers all asset and software types in scope.
evidence: Configuration management policy document

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process for Network Infrastructure
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a secure configuration process for network devices. Review and update documentation annually.
achieved: Network device baselines are defined and applied at provisioning.
Baseline compliance is verified during change management.
evidence: Network device hardening baseline document
Network device configuration audit report

items.name: Configure Automatic Session Locking on Enterprise Assets
items.desc: [IG1] Configure automatic session locking on enterprise assets after a defined period of inactivity. For general purpose operating systems, the period must not exceed 15 minutes. For mobile end-user devices, the period must not exceed 2 minutes.
achieved: Screen lock timeout is enforced via GPO or MDM on all managed devices.
Mobile devices lock after no more than 2 minutes of inactivity.
evidence: GPO/MDM screen lock policy configuration

items.name: Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers
items.desc: [IG1] Implement and manage a firewall on servers, where supported. Example implementations include a virtual firewall, operating system firewall, or a third-party firewall agent.
achieved: Host-based firewalls are enabled and configured on all servers.
Firewall rules follow least-privilege and default-deny principles.
evidence: Server firewall configuration baseline
Firewall rule audit report

items.name: Implement and Manage a Firewall on End-User Devices
items.desc: [IG1] Implement and manage a host-based firewall on end-user devices, with a default-deny rule that drops all traffic except those services and ports that are explicitly allowed.
achieved: Host-based firewall is enforced on all end-user devices via MDM or GPO.
Default-deny inbound policy is applied.
evidence: MDM/GPO firewall policy configuration report

items.name: Securely Manage Enterprise Assets and Software
items.desc: [IG2] Securely manage enterprise assets and software. Manage the security configuration of enterprise assets and software using an enterprise patch management system, configuration manager, or equivalent.
achieved: Enterprise management tooling (e.g. SCCM, Intune, Ansible) deploys and enforces configurations.
Configuration drift is detected and remediated within defined SLA.
evidence: Endpoint/configuration management tool coverage report
Drift remediation ticket samples

items.name: Manage Default Accounts on Enterprise Assets and Software
items.desc: [IG1] Manage default accounts on enterprise assets and software. Example implementations include disabling default accounts, or making them unusable.
achieved: All default accounts are disabled, renamed, or their passwords changed before deployment.
No default credentials remain active on production assets.
evidence: Hardening checklist showing default account remediation
Privileged account audit report

items.name: Uninstall or Disable Unnecessary Services on Enterprise Assets and Software
items.desc: [IG2] Uninstall or disable unnecessary services on enterprise assets and software, such as an unused file sharing service, web application module, or service function.
achieved: Only required services are enabled; all others are disabled.
Service inventory is reviewed when configurations change.
evidence: Hardening baseline showing disabled services
Vulnerability scan report confirming no unnecessary services

items.name: Configure Trusted DNS Servers on Enterprise Assets
items.desc: [IG2] Configure trusted DNS servers on enterprise assets. Example implementations include configuring assets to use enterprise-controlled DNS servers and/or reputable externally accessible DNS servers.
achieved: All assets use enterprise-approved DNS servers.
Rogue DNS configuration is detected via monitoring.
evidence: DNS configuration policy
DHCP/DNS server configuration export

items.name: Enforce Automatic Device Lockout on Portable End-User Devices
items.desc: [IG2] Enforce automatic device lockout following a predetermined threshold of local failed authentication attempts on portable end-user devices, where supported. For laptops, do not allow more than 20 failed authentication attempts; for tablets and smartphones, no more than 10 failed authentication attempts.
achieved: Account lockout policy is enforced on all portable devices via MDM.
Lockout thresholds are set at or below defined maximums.
evidence: MDM lockout policy configuration

items.name: Enforce Remote Wipe Capability on Portable End-User Devices
items.desc: [IG2] Remotely wipe enterprise data from enterprise-owned portable end-user devices when deemed appropriate such as lost or stolen devices, or when an individual no longer supports the enterprise.
achieved: Remote wipe capability is provisioned for all managed portable devices.
Remote wipe can be initiated within a defined timeframe.
evidence: MDM remote wipe capability evidence
Sample wipe request/confirmation tickets

items.name: Separate Enterprise Workspaces on Mobile End-User Devices
items.desc: [IG3] Ensure separate enterprise workspaces are used on mobile end-user devices where supported. Example implementations include using an MDM system to enable separation such as Apple Business Manager or Android for Work.
achieved: Enterprise data is containerised and separated from personal data on BYOD devices.
Container policies are enforced via MDM.
evidence: MDM container policy configuration
Coverage report for enrolled BYOD devices

groups.name: Account Management
groups.desc: Use processes and tools to assign and manage authorisation to credentials for user accounts, including administrator accounts, as well as service and application accounts.
achieved: All accounts are provisioned through a formal request and approval process.
Dormant and orphaned accounts are identified and disabled within a defined timeframe.
Privileged accounts are separate from standard user accounts.
Account inventory is reviewed at least quarterly.
evidence: Account provisioning process documentation and approval records
Dormant account report showing accounts disabled within SLA
Privileged account register
Quarterly access review evidence

items.name: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Accounts
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain an inventory of all accounts managed in the enterprise. The inventory must include both user and administrator accounts. Validate that all active accounts are authorised on a recurring schedule at a minimum quarterly, or more frequently.
achieved: Account inventory is complete and reviewed at least quarterly.
Inactive accounts are identified and actioned.

items.name: Use Unique Passwords

Evidence of separate user accounts for admins

items.name: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Accounts
items.desc: [IG2] Establish and maintain an inventory of service accounts. The inventory, at a minimum, must contain department owner, review date, and purpose. Service accounts are reviewed at least quarterly.
evidence: Service account inventory register
Quarterly review evidence

items.name: Centralise Account Management
items.desc: [IG2] Centralise account management through a directory or identity service.
achieved: All accounts are managed through a central directory (e.g. Azure AD, LDAP).

Local account audit showing only approved exceptions

groups.name: Access Control Management
groups.desc: Use processes and tools to create, assign, manage, and revoke access credentials and privileges for user, administrator, and service/application accounts.

The principle of least privilege is demonstrably enforced.

MFA enforcement policy and coverage report
Privilege access review records
Least-privilege access audit evidence

items.name: Establish an Access Granting Process
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and follow a process, preferably automated, for granting access to enterprise assets upon new hire, rights grant, or role change of a subject.

items.name: Require MFA for Externally-Exposed Applications

items.name: Require MFA for Administrative Access

Admin account MFA coverage report

items.name: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Authentication and Authorisation Systems
items.desc: [IG2] Establish and maintain an inventory of the enterprise's authentication and authorisation systems, including those hosted on-site or at a remote service provider. Review the inventory, at a minimum, annually.

evidence: AuthN/AuthZ system inventory register

items.name: Centralise Access Control

Application authentication inventory

items.name: Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control
items.desc: [IG3] Define and maintain role-based access control, through determining and documenting the access rights necessary for each role within the enterprise to successfully carry out its assigned duties. Semi-annual access review records

groups.name: Continuous Vulnerability Management

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Vulnerability Management Process
items.desc: [IG1] Establish and maintain a documented vulnerability management process for enterprise assets. Review and update documentation annually, or when significant enterprise changes occur that could impact this Safeguard.

items.name: Establish and Maintain a Remediation Process

items.name: Perform Automated Operating System Patch Management

items.name: Perform Automated Application Patch Management

items.name: Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Internal Enterprise Assets

items.name: Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Externally-Exposed Enterprise Assets

items.name: Remediate Detected Vulnerabilities

items.name: Collect Audit Logs

items.name: Collect Command-Line Audit Logs

items.name: Centralise Audit Logs

items.name: Collect Service Provider Logs

groups.name: Email and Web Browser Protections

items.name: Establish and Maintain an Enterprise Process for Reporting Incidents

desc.Req 1: Install and Maintain Network Security Controls — Requirement 1 requires organisations to establish and maintain network security controls (NSCs) — firewalls, routers, and equivalent devices — that restrict inbound and outbound network traffic to that which is necessary for the cardholder data environment (CDE). All NSC rule sets must be documented, reviewed at least every six months, and default deny rules applied. Network diagrams must be maintained showing all connections between the CDE and other networks.
desc.Req 2: Apply Secure Configurations to All System Components — Requirement 2 requires that all system components within the CDE are configured securely from deployment. Vendor-supplied defaults (default passwords, unnecessary services, default accounts) must be changed or disabled before systems are placed in production. Configuration standards must be developed based on industry-accepted hardening guidance (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, NIST guidelines) and applied consistently.
desc.Req 3: Protect Stored Account Data — Requirement 3 requires that stored cardholder data is minimised and protected. The primary account number (PAN) must be rendered unreadable anywhere it is stored using strong cryptography, truncation, tokenisation, or one-way hashing. Sensitive authentication data (SAD) — including full track data, CVV/CVC codes, and PINs — must never be stored after authorisation, regardless of encryption. A data retention and disposal policy must define the minimum data storage needed.
desc.Req 4: Protect Cardholder Data with Strong Cryptography During Transmission Over Open, Public Networks — Requirement 4 requires that cardholder data (particularly PAN) is protected using strong cryptography during transmission over open or public networks. Only trusted keys and certificates must be used, and TLS 1.2 or higher must be implemented. The use of end-user messaging technologies (email, SMS, chat) to transmit unprotected PAN is prohibited.
desc.Req 5: Protect All Systems and Networks from Malicious Software — Requirement 5 requires that all systems — particularly those commonly affected by malware — are protected by anti-malware solutions. Anti-malware software must be kept current, generate audit logs, and actively run. The requirement now extends to all components in the CDE, not just those traditionally targeted by malware, with a risk-based evaluation for components where malware risk is low.
desc.Req 6: Develop and Maintain Secure Systems and Software — Requirement 6 requires that all system components are protected from known vulnerabilities and that software developed by or for the organisation follows a secure development lifecycle (SDLC). This includes applying security patches within defined timeframes, identifying vulnerabilities through code review and security testing, and training developers in secure coding techniques.
desc.Req 7: Restrict Access to System Components and Cardholder Data by Business Need to Know — Requirement 7 requires that access to cardholder data and CDE system components is limited to only those individuals whose job requires such access. This is achieved through formal access control systems, role-based access policies, and the principle of least privilege. Access to all system components must be managed through an access control system that enforces deny-all by default.
desc.Req 8: Identify Users and Authenticate Access to System Components — Requirement 8 requires that all users are uniquely identified and that strong authentication mechanisms are used. Shared or generic accounts are prohibited. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for all non-console access into the CDE and for all remote access. Passwords and passphrases must meet complexity and length requirements, and account lockout thresholds must be set.
desc.Req 9: Restrict Physical Access to Cardholder Data — Requirement 9 requires that physical access to systems that store, process, or transmit cardholder data is restricted to authorised individuals. This includes secure data centre access controls, visitor management, protection of physical media, and secure disposal of media containing cardholder data.
desc.Req 10: Log and Monitor All Access to System Components and Cardholder Data — Requirement 10 requires that all access to CDE system components, particularly access by administrators and access to cardholder data, is logged and the logs are monitored for anomalies and suspicious activity. Audit logs must be protected from destruction and modification, retained for at least 12 months with at least three months immediately available, and reviewed daily.
desc.Req 11: Test Security of Systems and Networks Regularly — Requirement 11 requires that the security of CDE systems and networks is tested regularly through vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, intrusion detection, and change detection. Internal and external vulnerability scans must be performed quarterly. Penetration testing must be performed at least annually and after any significant CDE changes. A change-detection mechanism must monitor critical files for unauthorised modifications.
desc.Req 12: Support Information Security with Organisational Policies and Programs — Requirement 12 addresses the governance and organisational foundations of the PCI DSS programme. It requires a comprehensive information security policy, acceptable use policies, risk assessments, security awareness training, incident response capability, vendor management, and executive accountability for PCI DSS compliance. The requirement emphasises that security is an ongoing organisational commitment, not a point-in-time exercise.

about.title: About PCI DSS 4.0
about.blurb: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is a global security standard established by the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC) and required by card brands including Visa, Mastercard, and American Express. Version 4.0 (updated to 4.0.1) was released in 2022 and introduces a customised approach alongside the traditional defined approach, giving organisations greater flexibility to demonstrate equivalent security outcomes. Compliance is mandatory for any organisation that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, and is validated annually through a Report on Compliance (ROC) completed by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) or a Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) depending on transaction volumes. PCI DSS 4.0 significantly emphasises security as a continuous process rather than a point-in-time assessment.

desc.Firewalls: Firewalls — The Firewalls theme requires organisations to protect all devices that can be connected to the internet, whether directly or via a home or public network, using boundary firewalls and internet gateways. All devices must have a software firewall or host-based firewall enabled. The default firewall configuration must block all traffic that has not been explicitly permitted, and rules must be documented and reviewed regularly. Unapproved services must not be exposed to the internet.
desc.Firewalls.1: Boundary firewall protection at all internet connections — A boundary firewall or equivalent control is deployed at every connection between the organisation's internal network and the internet, ensuring all traffic passes through an approved security control point.
desc.Firewalls.2: Firewall rule documentation and review — All firewall rules permitting traffic are documented with a clear business justification, and the rule set is reviewed at least annually to remove rules that are no longer required.
desc.Firewalls.3: Host-based software firewall on all devices — A software firewall is enabled on all organisation-managed devices, blocking all inbound connections that have not been explicitly permitted.
desc.Secure Config: Secure Configuration — The Secure Configuration theme requires that all organisation-managed computers and network devices are configured to reduce the attack surface. Unnecessary software, services, and user accounts must be removed or disabled. Vendor-supplied default passwords must be changed before devices are put into use. Only approved and necessary software should be installed on devices, and auto-run features that automatically execute code from removable media should be disabled.
desc.Secure Config.1: Default password changes on all devices and software — Vendor-supplied default passwords on all internet-connected devices, accounts, and software are changed to unique, strong passwords before the device or software is put into use.
desc.Secure Config.2: Disable unnecessary services and open ports — All services, protocols, and open network ports that are not required for the device's function are disabled or removed to reduce the attack surface.
desc.Secure Config.3: Restrict software installation to authorised software only — Users are prevented from installing software that has not been approved by the organisation, and a process exists to manage and review what software is installed across the estate.
desc.Access Control: Access Control — The Access Control theme requires that user accounts are created and maintained on the basis of least privilege, with access limited to what is needed for the user's role. Administrative accounts must be used only for administrative tasks and must be separate from standard user accounts. Multi-factor authentication must be enabled for all accounts that can access cloud services, administrator accounts, and accounts accessing data or services exposed to the internet. Unused accounts must be removed or disabled promptly.
desc.Access Control.1: User account management and least privilege — User accounts are created with only the privileges needed for the individual's role, and privilege is reviewed and adjusted when roles change.
desc.Access Control.2: Multi-factor authentication for all applicable accounts — Multi-factor authentication is enabled for all user and administrator accounts that access cloud services, administrator interfaces, and internet-facing data or services.
desc.Access Control.3: Separate administrative accounts — Administrative privileges are used only via dedicated administrative accounts, separate from the user's standard day-to-day account, and used only for administrative tasks.
desc.Access Control.4: Prompt removal of unused accounts — User accounts that are no longer required (for example, because a user has left the organisation or a service has been decommissioned) are removed or disabled promptly.
desc.Malware Protection: Malware Protection — The Malware Protection theme requires that organisation-managed devices are protected against malware using one or more of: anti-malware software, application allow-listing, or sandboxing. Anti-malware software must be kept up to date, must be actively running, and must perform regular scans or real-time protection. Devices that are not covered by anti-malware must be covered by application allow-listing as an alternative approach, which the NCSC considers equally or more effective.
desc.Malware Protection.1: Anti-malware software deployed and actively running — Anti-malware or endpoint detection and response software is deployed on all organisation-managed devices, is running with real-time protection enabled, and is configured to prevent users from disabling it.
desc.Malware Protection.2: Web filtering to block access to malicious sites — Web content filtering is in place to prevent users from accessing known malicious websites and to reduce the risk of malware delivery via web browsing.
desc.Malware Protection.3: Application allow-listing as an alternative or supplementary control — Where anti-malware software is not deployed, or as a supplementary control, application allow-listing is implemented to prevent the execution of unapproved software on devices.
desc.Security Updates: Security Updates — The Security Updates theme requires that all software, operating systems, and firmware on in-scope devices are kept up to date to address known security vulnerabilities. High and critical severity patches must be applied within 14 days of release. Software that is no longer supported by the vendor (end-of-life or end-of-support) and that cannot be patched must be removed from the scope of the Cyber Essentials assessment or protected by compensating controls. Automatic updates should be enabled where possible.
desc.Security Updates.1: 14-day patching SLA for high and critical vulnerabilities — Security patches rated high or critical severity are applied to all in-scope devices within 14 days of the patch becoming available from the vendor.
desc.Security Updates.2: Operating system, firmware, and application updates applied — Security updates are applied to all in-scope software categories: operating systems, firmware (BIOS, UEFI, network device firmware), and third-party applications.
desc.Security Updates.3: Unsupported software removed or risk-accepted — Software, operating systems, and firmware that are no longer supported by the vendor and no longer receive security updates are removed from in-scope devices. Where removal is not possible, a formal risk acceptance is documented and compensating controls are applied.

about.title: About Cyber Essentials
about.blurb: Cyber Essentials is a UK government-backed certification scheme, managed by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and delivered through accredited certification bodies. It defines a baseline of five technical security controls designed to protect organisations against the most common cyber threats, which the NCSC assesses account for the majority of cyber attacks. Cyber Essentials (self-assessed) and Cyber Essentials Plus (independently assessed through technical verification) are both recognised certifications. From April 2026, the scheme operates under version 3.3 of the requirements. Certification is mandatory for organisations bidding for certain UK government contracts involving the handling of sensitive information and personal data. The scheme is intentionally accessible and achievable for organisations of all sizes.
