desc.§5: Information Security Policies — Section 5 covers information security policies for cloud services. Cloud customers should include cloud-specific provisions in their information security policy, addressing acceptable use of cloud services, classification of data stored in the cloud, and responsibilities under the shared responsibility model.
desc.§6: Organisation of Information Security — Section 6 covers the organisation of information security for cloud environments. A key cloud-specific addition is CLD.6.3, which addresses the need to explicitly document and agree the division of security responsibilities between cloud service provider and customer.
desc.CLD.6.3: Shared roles and responsibilities within a cloud computing environment — The relationship and the division of information security roles and responsibilities between the cloud service provider and the cloud service customer should be designed and documented. Cloud customers must understand which security controls are the responsibility of the provider, which are shared, and which are solely the customer's responsibility.
desc.§7: Human Resource Security — Section 7 covers human resource security in cloud environments. Cloud service providers must ensure their personnel who manage cloud infrastructure and customer data are appropriately screened and trained. Cloud customers should ensure their policies extend to cloud operations personnel.
desc.§8: Asset Management — Section 8 covers asset management in cloud environments, including the management of assets held in or managed by cloud services. CLD.8.1.5 addresses the specific requirement for cloud providers to return or delete customer assets on termination of service.
desc.CLD.8.1.5: Removal of cloud service customer assets — The cloud service provider should have a process for the return or secure deletion of cloud service customer assets upon termination of service. Customers should verify this through contractual requirements and by requesting evidence of deletion. The process should address all data including copies, backups, and replicas.
desc.§9: Access Control — Section 9 covers access control for cloud environments. Two cloud-specific controls address the unique challenges of multi-tenancy: CLD.9.5.1 covers segregation between virtual environments shared by multiple customers, and CLD.9.5.2 covers hardening of virtual machine instances.
desc.CLD.9.5.1: Segregation in virtual computing environments — Cloud service providers must ensure that virtual computing environments belonging to different cloud service customers are segregated from each other to prevent unauthorised access and data leakage between tenants. Cloud customers should verify this segregation through provider assurance documentation and consider additional controls where sensitive data is involved.
desc.CLD.9.5.2: Virtual machine hardening — Virtual machine images should be hardened to reduce the attack surface. Only necessary services should be enabled, default credentials removed, and configuration aligned with approved security baselines. Hardened base images should be maintained and used for all VM provisioning.
desc.§10: Cryptography — Section 10 covers cryptographic controls for cloud environments. Organisations using cloud services must ensure data is encrypted at rest and in transit and that key management arrangements preserve the confidentiality and integrity of cryptographic keys, particularly where the cloud provider holds keys on the customer's behalf.
desc.§11: Physical and Environmental Security — Section 11 covers physical and environmental security in the context of cloud service provision. For cloud customers, the provider is responsible for physical security of infrastructure; customers should verify this through provider assurance documentation. Cloud providers must protect their data centre facilities to a high standard.
desc.§12: Operations Security — Section 12 covers operational security for cloud environments, including two cloud-specific controls: CLD.12.1.5 on the security of administrator operations within cloud environments, and CLD.12.4.5 on monitoring the cloud service itself.
desc.CLD.12.1.5: Administrator's operational security — Cloud service providers should ensure that administrator access to cloud infrastructure is tightly controlled, logged, and monitored. All administrative activities should be performed using dedicated privileged accounts with MFA, and all actions should generate immutable audit logs. Cloud customers should implement equivalent controls for their cloud management plane access.
desc.CLD.12.4.5: Monitoring of cloud services — The cloud service customer should monitor the cloud service to detect anomalous behaviour, security events, and misconfigurations. Monitoring should cover authentication events, configuration changes, data access patterns, and network traffic. Cloud-native monitoring tools should be supplemented with SIEM integration.
desc.§13: Communications Security — Section 13 covers communications security for cloud environments. CLD.13.1.4 addresses the specific challenge of securing network connections in virtualised environments where traditional physical network controls do not apply.
desc.CLD.13.1.4: Security management of networks for virtual and physical networks — The network security management for cloud environments should address both virtual networks (SDN, VPC, VNET) and physical network connections. Security groups and network ACLs should be configured on a default-deny basis. Virtual network flows should be logged and monitored.
desc.§14: System Acquisition, Development and Maintenance — Section 14 covers secure development and acquisition in cloud environments. Cloud service customers should apply secure development practices to cloud-native applications, including secure configuration of cloud services used as application components (object storage, queues, databases, serverless functions).
desc.§15: Supplier Relationships — Section 15 covers supplier relationships in cloud environments. Cloud service providers are key suppliers and must be assessed and managed through the supplier management framework. Service level agreements with cloud providers should include security obligations.
desc.§16: Information Security Incident Management — Section 16 covers incident management in cloud environments. CLD.16.1.3 requires that security events detected by the cloud service provider that affect the customer are notified promptly. Cloud customers should ensure their incident response procedures account for cloud-hosted assets and involve cloud provider support.
desc.CLD.16.1.3: Security event notification by cloud service providers — The cloud service provider should have a process for notifying customers of security events that may affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of their data or services. Customers should contractually specify notification timelines and define their own procedures for receiving and acting on such notifications.
desc.§17: Information Security Aspects of Business Continuity Management — Section 17 covers information security continuity in cloud environments. CLD.17.1.1 addresses the specific need to plan for information security continuity scenarios involving the cloud service provider, including provider outages, insolvency, or security incidents at the provider.
desc.CLD.17.1.1: Information security continuity in a cloud computing environment — Cloud service customers should plan for information security continuity in scenarios involving disruption to or unavailability of cloud services. This includes provider outages, regulatory action, provider insolvency, and security incidents at the provider. Continuity plans should address alternative providers or on-premises fallback, data portability, and backup restoration.
desc.§18: Compliance — Section 18 covers compliance in cloud environments. Organisations must identify and comply with legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements applicable to their cloud-hosted data, including data residency, privacy regulations, and sector-specific compliance obligations.

about.title: ISO/IEC 27017:2015 — Code of Practice for Cloud Services
about.blurb: ISO/IEC 27017 provides guidelines for information security controls applicable to the provision and use of cloud services. It supplements ISO/IEC 27002 by providing additional implementation guidance for cloud-specific controls and introducing seven new cloud-only controls (CLD controls) not found in ISO 27002.

p: 27017 maps to ISO 27002:2013 sections (§5–§18). For each section it provides cloud-specific implementation guidance for existing controls and, where cloud scenarios introduce unique risks, adds new CLD.x.x controls.

sections.h: Cloud service customer vs. cloud service provider
p: Each control distinguishes between obligations for the cloud service customer (CSC — the organisation using cloud services) and the cloud service provider (CSP — the entity offering cloud services). Many organisations will be both simultaneously.

groups.name: Information Security Policies
groups.desc: Section 5 covers information security policies for cloud services. Cloud customers should include cloud-specific provisions in their information security policy, addressing acceptable use of cloud services, classification of data stored in the cloud, and responsibilities under the shared responsibility model.
achieved: Information security policy addresses cloud service usage, acceptable use, and data classification.
Cloud-specific security requirements are documented and communicated to relevant personnel.
Policy is reviewed when new cloud services are adopted or when the cloud environment materially changes.
evidence: Information security policy with cloud service provisions
Cloud acceptable use policy or cloud security addendum
Policy review records following cloud service adoption

groups.name: Organisation of Information Security
groups.desc: Section 6 covers the organisation of information security for cloud environments. A key cloud-specific addition is CLD.6.3, which addresses the need to explicitly document and agree the division of security responsibilities between cloud service provider and customer.
achieved: Roles and responsibilities for cloud security are defined and assigned.
Shared responsibility boundaries with each cloud provider are documented and agreed.
Security contacts within cloud providers are identified and maintained.
Remote working security requirements address cloud access from off-premises locations.
evidence: Cloud shared responsibility model documentation per provider (CLD.6.3)
RACI for cloud security roles including CSP and CSC responsibilities
Remote working policy covering cloud service access

items.name: Shared roles and responsibilities within a cloud computing environment
items.desc: The relationship and the division of information security roles and responsibilities between the cloud service provider and the cloud service customer should be designed and documented. Cloud customers must understand which security controls are the responsibility of the provider, which are shared, and which are solely the customer's responsibility.
achieved: A shared responsibility matrix is documented for each cloud provider in use.
Customer-managed security controls are identified and implemented.
Provider-managed controls are verified through the provider's compliance documentation (SOC 2, ISO 27001 certificate).
evidence: Shared responsibility matrix per cloud provider
Provider compliance certificates or SOC 2 reports
Internal control implementation evidence for customer-managed responsibilities

groups.name: Human Resource Security
groups.desc: Section 7 covers human resource security in cloud environments. Cloud service providers must ensure their personnel who manage cloud infrastructure and customer data are appropriately screened and trained. Cloud customers should ensure their policies extend to cloud operations personnel.
achieved: Personnel with access to cloud management planes are screened appropriately.
Cloud-specific security training is included in awareness programmes.
Offboarding procedures ensure timely revocation of cloud access credentials.
Contractors and third parties with cloud access are subject to equivalent personnel security requirements.
evidence: Screening records for cloud operations personnel
Cloud security training module completion records
Offboarding checklist showing cloud access revocation

groups.name: Asset Management
groups.desc: Section 8 covers asset management in cloud environments, including the management of assets held in or managed by cloud services. CLD.8.1.5 addresses the specific requirement for cloud providers to return or delete customer assets on termination of service.
achieved: Cloud-hosted assets (data, virtual machines, containers, storage) are inventoried and owned.
Data classification is applied to assets stored in cloud services.
Procedures are in place to ensure return or deletion of customer data on service termination.
Acceptable use requirements for cloud services are documented and communicated.
evidence: Cloud asset inventory covering data stores, compute, and storage
Data classification labels applied to cloud-stored data
Contract and procedure for data return/deletion on termination (CLD.8.1.5)

items.name: Removal of cloud service customer assets
items.desc: The cloud service provider should have a process for the return or secure deletion of cloud service customer assets upon termination of service. Customers should verify this through contractual requirements and by requesting evidence of deletion. The process should address all data including copies, backups, and replicas.
achieved: Contract specifies the provider's obligations for data return/deletion on termination.
Customer has a documented procedure for initiating and verifying data removal.
Evidence of deletion or return is obtained and retained after termination.
evidence: Contract clause specifying data deletion/return obligations
Data deletion request procedure
Deletion confirmation or certificate from cloud provider following termination

groups.name: Access Control
groups.desc: Section 9 covers access control for cloud environments. Two cloud-specific controls address the unique challenges of multi-tenancy: CLD.9.5.1 covers segregation between virtual environments shared by multiple customers, and CLD.9.5.2 covers hardening of virtual machine instances.
achieved: Access to cloud management consoles and APIs is controlled using least-privilege and MFA.
Logical segregation between the organisation's cloud environment and other tenants is verified.
Virtual machine instances are hardened per defined baselines.
Privileged access to cloud resources is managed through a PAM solution.
Cloud access control policies are reviewed when the cloud configuration materially changes.
evidence: Cloud IAM configuration showing least-privilege roles and MFA enforcement
Segregation evidence from provider (SOC 2 report, shared responsibility documentation)
VM hardening baseline and compliance scan results
PAM tool configuration for cloud privileged access

items.name: Segregation in virtual computing environments
items.desc: Cloud service providers must ensure that virtual computing environments belonging to different cloud service customers are segregated from each other to prevent unauthorised access and data leakage between tenants. Cloud customers should verify this segregation through provider assurance documentation and consider additional controls where sensitive data is involved.
achieved: Provider's multi-tenancy isolation is verified through SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification.
Network-level isolation (VPCs, VNETs, security groups) is configured to separate the organisation's resources.
Dedicated infrastructure options are used where regulatory requirements demand physical separation.
evidence: Cloud provider SOC 2 report confirming tenant isolation controls
VPC/VNET configuration showing network isolation
Dedicated tenancy configuration where required

items.name: Virtual machine hardening
items.desc: Virtual machine images should be hardened to reduce the attack surface. Only necessary services should be enabled, default credentials removed, and configuration aligned with approved security baselines. Hardened base images should be maintained and used for all VM provisioning.
achieved: Hardened VM images or AMIs are maintained and used as the standard for all provisioning.
Hardening baseline is aligned with CIS Benchmarks for the OS.
VM configuration compliance is monitored continuously.
Deviations from baselines are remediated within defined SLAs.
evidence: Hardened base image documentation and CIS Benchmark alignment
VM configuration compliance scan reports
Image pipeline showing hardening steps in build process

groups.name: Cryptography
groups.desc: Section 10 covers cryptographic controls for cloud environments. Organisations using cloud services must ensure data is encrypted at rest and in transit and that key management arrangements preserve the confidentiality and integrity of cryptographic keys, particularly where the cloud provider holds keys on the customer's behalf.
achieved: Data stored in cloud services is encrypted at rest using customer-managed or provider-managed keys.
Data in transit to and within cloud services uses TLS 1.2 or higher.
Key management policy covers cloud key management and customer-managed key (CMK) usage.
Access to encryption keys is tightly controlled and audited.
evidence: Cloud storage encryption configuration (at-rest encryption enabled)
TLS configuration for cloud service endpoints
Customer-managed key (CMK) configuration in KMS where required
Key access audit log evidence

groups.name: Physical and Environmental Security
groups.desc: Section 11 covers physical and environmental security in the context of cloud service provision. For cloud customers, the provider is responsible for physical security of infrastructure; customers should verify this through provider assurance documentation. Cloud providers must protect their data centre facilities to a high standard.
achieved: Cloud provider's physical security controls are verified through SOC 2, ISO 27001, or equivalent assurance.
Physical access to on-premises assets connecting to cloud services is controlled.
Data residency requirements are defined and verified against provider capabilities.
evidence: Cloud provider SOC 2/ISO 27001 certificate confirming physical security
Data residency configuration evidence showing data remains within required geography
Physical access controls for on-premises cloud connectivity equipment

groups.name: Operations Security
groups.desc: Section 12 covers operational security for cloud environments, including two cloud-specific controls: CLD.12.1.5 on the security of administrator operations within cloud environments, and CLD.12.4.5 on monitoring the cloud service itself.
achieved: Cloud operational procedures cover change management, capacity, and backup.
Administrators managing cloud infrastructure operate under least-privilege principles with all actions logged.
Cloud service monitoring provides visibility into the security posture of cloud resources.
Vulnerability management extends to cloud-hosted workloads.
Logs from cloud services are centralised and reviewed.
evidence: Cloud change management process covering infrastructure-as-code deployments
Cloud administrator activity logs and privileged access records
Cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool deployment evidence
Cloud vulnerability scan reports

items.name: Administrator's operational security
items.desc: Cloud service providers should ensure that administrator access to cloud infrastructure is tightly controlled, logged, and monitored. All administrative activities should be performed using dedicated privileged accounts with MFA, and all actions should generate immutable audit logs. Cloud customers should implement equivalent controls for their cloud management plane access.
achieved: Cloud console and API access for administrators requires MFA.
Privileged cloud operations use dedicated accounts with session recording.
All cloud administrative actions are logged to an immutable audit trail.
Logs are retained for at least 12 months and reviewed for anomalies.
evidence: Cloud IAM MFA enforcement for privileged roles
CloudTrail/Azure Activity Log/GCP Audit Log configuration showing all API calls captured
Log retention configuration showing 12-month retention
Privileged access management configuration for cloud operations

items.name: Monitoring of cloud services
items.desc: The cloud service customer should monitor the cloud service to detect anomalous behaviour, security events, and misconfigurations. Monitoring should cover authentication events, configuration changes, data access patterns, and network traffic. Cloud-native monitoring tools should be supplemented with SIEM integration.
achieved: Cloud-native monitoring (GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud, Security Command Center) is enabled.
Cloud audit logs are forwarded to SIEM for correlation with other security events.
Alerts are configured for high-risk cloud events (e.g. root account use, public exposure, privilege escalation).
CSPM tool continuously monitors for cloud misconfiguration.
evidence: Cloud-native security monitoring service configuration
SIEM integration showing cloud log ingestion
Alert rules for high-risk cloud events
CSPM misconfiguration scan reports

groups.name: Communications Security
groups.desc: Section 13 covers communications security for cloud environments. CLD.13.1.4 addresses the specific challenge of securing network connections in virtualised environments where traditional physical network controls do not apply.
achieved: Network security groups and virtual firewalls are configured to restrict traffic to required flows only.
Virtual networks are segmented to isolate sensitive workloads.
Network traffic within and between cloud environments is monitored.
Encrypted tunnels (VPN, ExpressRoute, Direct Connect) are used for connectivity to cloud environments.
evidence: Cloud network security group and firewall rule configuration
Virtual network architecture diagram showing segmentation
Encrypted connectivity configuration (VPN/private peering) documentation

items.name: Security management of networks for virtual and physical networks
items.desc: The network security management for cloud environments should address both virtual networks (SDN, VPC, VNET) and physical network connections. Security groups and network ACLs should be configured on a default-deny basis. Virtual network flows should be logged and monitored.
achieved: All cloud network security groups implement a default-deny inbound policy.
VPC/VNET flow logs are enabled and forwarded to SIEM.
Network security rules are reviewed at least quarterly for unnecessary permissions.
East-west traffic between cloud workloads is monitored using cloud-native NDR or traffic mirroring.
evidence: Cloud network security group configuration showing default-deny rules
VPC Flow Log / NSG Flow Log configuration
Quarterly network rule review records
East-west monitoring configuration or traffic analysis evidence

groups.name: System Acquisition, Development and Maintenance
groups.desc: Section 14 covers secure development and acquisition in cloud environments. Cloud service customers should apply secure development practices to cloud-native applications, including secure configuration of cloud services used as application components (object storage, queues, databases, serverless functions).
achieved: Security requirements address cloud-native components (storage permissions, API gateways, serverless).
Infrastructure-as-code is used to deploy cloud resources with security baselines enforced at provisioning.
Static analysis of infrastructure code (IaC scanning) identifies misconfigurations before deployment.
Cloud application penetration testing is conducted at least annually.
evidence: Cloud security requirements in development standards
IaC templates with security controls and IaC scan results
Cloud application penetration test reports

groups.name: Supplier Relationships
groups.desc: Section 15 covers supplier relationships in cloud environments. Cloud service providers are key suppliers and must be assessed and managed through the supplier management framework. Service level agreements with cloud providers should include security obligations.
achieved: Cloud service providers are assessed as part of the supplier risk management process.
Cloud provider SLAs and contractual terms are reviewed for security obligations.
Shared responsibility models are agreed and documented per provider.
Cloud provider security posture is monitored through their published compliance programmes.
evidence: Cloud provider risk assessment records
Cloud provider contracts and SLA documentation with security clauses
Shared responsibility model documentation
Cloud provider compliance certification evidence (SOC 2, ISO 27001, CSA STAR)

groups.name: Information Security Incident Management
groups.desc: Section 16 covers incident management in cloud environments. CLD.16.1.3 requires that security events detected by the cloud service provider that affect the customer are notified promptly. Cloud customers should ensure their incident response procedures account for cloud-hosted assets and involve cloud provider support.
achieved: Incident response procedures address cloud-specific scenarios (cloud account compromise, data exposure, CSP-side incident).
Cloud providers are contractually required to notify the organisation of security incidents affecting them.
Cloud-native alerts feed into the incident detection and response workflow.
Post-incident reviews for cloud incidents identify cloud-specific improvements.
evidence: Incident response plan with cloud-specific playbooks
Contract clause requiring CSP incident notification
Cloud security alert integration with SIEM/ticketing system

items.name: Security event notification by cloud service providers
items.desc: The cloud service provider should have a process for notifying customers of security events that may affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of their data or services. Customers should contractually specify notification timelines and define their own procedures for receiving and acting on such notifications.
achieved: Cloud provider contract specifies incident notification timelines (e.g. within 24 hours of detection).
A designated contact is published to the cloud provider for security notifications.
Received notifications trigger the organisation's incident response process.
Provider security notification history is reviewed during annual supplier reviews.
evidence: Contract clause specifying CSP incident notification obligations
Security contact registration with cloud provider
Records of CSP security notifications received and actioned

groups.name: Information Security Aspects of Business Continuity Management
groups.desc: Section 17 covers information security continuity in cloud environments. CLD.17.1.1 addresses the specific need to plan for information security continuity scenarios involving the cloud service provider, including provider outages, insolvency, or security incidents at the provider.
achieved: Business continuity plans address cloud service provider outage scenarios.
Recovery objectives for cloud-hosted services are defined and tested.
Portability and exit strategies are documented for critical cloud services.
Dependencies on single cloud providers are identified and mitigated where critical.
evidence: BCP covering cloud provider outage scenarios
DR test results for cloud-hosted critical services
Cloud exit strategy documentation

items.name: Information security continuity in a cloud computing environment
items.desc: Cloud service customers should plan for information security continuity in scenarios involving disruption to or unavailability of cloud services. This includes provider outages, regulatory action, provider insolvency, and security incidents at the provider. Continuity plans should address alternative providers or on-premises fallback, data portability, and backup restoration.
achieved: Continuity plans identify cloud provider dependency risks and document mitigation strategies.
Data is backed up in formats portable to alternative providers.
Multi-region or multi-provider architectures are used for critical services where justified by risk.
Provider outage scenarios are included in annual continuity exercises.
evidence: Business Continuity Plan sections addressing cloud provider outage
Cloud data portability and export evidence
Multi-region/provider architecture documentation for critical services
Continuity exercise records including cloud outage scenario

groups.name: Compliance
groups.desc: Section 18 covers compliance in cloud environments. Organisations must identify and comply with legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements applicable to their cloud-hosted data, including data residency, privacy regulations, and sector-specific compliance obligations.
achieved: Legal, regulatory, and contractual compliance requirements for cloud environments are identified.
Data residency requirements are documented and enforced through cloud configuration.
Independent reviews and audits extend to cloud-hosted systems.
Compliance evidence from cloud providers (SOC 2, ISO 27001, CSA STAR) is maintained.
evidence: Cloud compliance requirements register covering applicable regulations and standards
Data residency configuration evidence
Cloud provider compliance certificates and SOC 2 reports
Cloud penetration test or security assessment reports

desc.A1: Governance — The organisation has appropriate management policies, processes and procedures in place to govern its approach to the security of network and information systems.
desc.A1.a: Board Direction — You have effective organisational security management led at board level and articulated clearly in corresponding policies.
desc.A1.b: Roles and Responsibilities — Your organisation has established roles and responsibilities for the security of network and information systems at all levels, with clear and well-understood channels for communicating and escalating risks.
desc.A1.c: Decision-making — You have senior-level accountability for the security of network and information systems, and delegate decision-making authority appropriately and effectively. Risks to systems related to essential function(s) are considered in the context of other organisational risks.
desc.A2: Risk Management — The organisation takes appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand security risks to network and information systems supporting the operation of essential functions. This includes an overall organisational approach to risk management.
desc.A2.a: Risk Management Process — Your organisation has effective internal processes for managing risks to the security and resilience of network and information systems related to essential function(s) and communicating associated activities.
desc.A2.b: Understanding Threat — You understand the capabilities, methods and techniques of threat actors and what network and information systems they may compromise to adversely impact essential function(s). This information is used to inform security and resilience risk management decisions.
desc.A2.c: Assurance — You have gained confidence in the effectiveness of the security of your technology, people and processes relevant to the operation of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.A3: Asset Management — Everything required to deliver, maintain or support network and information systems necessary for essential functions is determined and understood. This includes data, people and systems, as well as supporting infrastructure (such as power or cooling).
desc.A3.a: Asset Management — All assets required to deliver, maintain or support essential function(s) are determined, understood, prioritised and managed throughout their lifecycle.
desc.A4: Supply Chain — The organisation understands and manages security risks to network and information systems supporting essential functions that arise as a result of dependencies on suppliers. This includes ensuring that appropriate measures are employed where third party services are used.
desc.A4.a: Supply Chain — You understand and effectively manage the risks associated with suppliers to the security of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.A4.b: Secure Software Development and Support — You actively maximise the use of secure and supported software, whether developed internally or sourced externally, within network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B1: Service Protection Policies, Processes and Procedures — The organisation defines, implements, communicates and enforces appropriate policies, processes and procedures that direct its overall approach to securing systems and data that support operation of essential functions.
desc.B1.a: Policy, Process and Procedure Development — You have developed and continue to improve a set of cyber security and resilience policies, processes and procedures that manage and mitigate the risk of adverse impact to network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B1.b: Policy, Process and Procedure Implementation — You have successfully implemented your security policies, processes and procedures and can demonstrate the security benefits achieved.
desc.B2: Identity and Access Control — The organisation understands, documents and manages access to network and information systems supporting essential functions. Users (or automated functions) that can access data or systems are appropriately verified, authenticated and authorised.
desc.B2.a: Identity Verification, Authentication and Authorisation — You robustly verify, authenticate and authorise access to network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B2.b: Device Management — You fully know and have trust in the devices that are used to access your networks, information systems and data that support essential function(s).
desc.B2.c: Privileged User Management — You closely manage privileged user access to network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B2.d: Identity and Access Management (IdAM) — You closely manage and maintain identity and access control for users, devices and systems accessing network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B3: Data Security — Data stored or transmitted electronically is protected from actions such as unauthorised access, modification, or deletion that may cause an adverse impact on essential functions.
desc.B3.a: Understanding Data — You have a good understanding of data important to network and information systems supporting essential function(s) — where it is stored, where it travels and how unavailability or unauthorised access, release, modification or deletion would adversely impact essential function(s).
desc.B3.b: Data in Transit — You have protected the transit of data important to network and information systems supporting essential function(s) (including transfers to third parties).
desc.B3.c: Stored Data — You have protected stored soft and hard copy data important to network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B3.d: Mobile Data — You have protected data important to network and information systems supporting essential function(s) on mobile devices (smartphones, tablets, laptops).
desc.B3.e: Media / Equipment Sanitisation — Before reuse and/or disposal you appropriately sanitise devices, equipment and removable media holding data important to essential function(s).
desc.B4: System Security — Network and information systems and technology critical for essential functions are protected from cyber attack. An organisational understanding of risk informs the use of robust and reliable protective security measures.
desc.B4.a: Secure by Design — You design security into network and information systems supporting essential function(s). You minimise their attack surface and ensure essential function(s) should not be impacted by exploitation of any single vulnerability.
desc.B4.b: Secure Configuration — You securely configure network and information systems that support essential function(s).
desc.B4.c: Secure Management — You manage your organisation's network and information systems that support essential function(s) to enable and maintain security.
desc.B4.d: Vulnerability Management — You manage known vulnerabilities in network and information systems to prevent adverse impact on essential function(s).
desc.B5: Resilient Networks and Systems — The organisation builds resilience against cyber attack and system failure into the design, implementation, operation and management of systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B5.a: Resilience Preparation — You are prepared to restore the operation of essential function(s) following adverse impact to network and information systems.
desc.B5.b: Design for Resilience — You design network and information systems supporting essential function(s) to be resilient to cyber security incidents. Systems are appropriately segregated and resource limitations are mitigated.
desc.B5.c: Backups — You hold accessible and secured current backups of data and information needed to recover operation of essential function(s) following adverse impact.
desc.B6: Staff Awareness and Training — Staff have appropriate awareness, knowledge and skills to carry out their organisational roles effectively in relation to the security of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.B6.a: Cyber Security Culture — You develop and maintain a positive cyber security culture and a shared sense of responsibility.
desc.B6.b: Cyber Security Training — The people who support the operation of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) are appropriately trained in cyber security.
desc.C1: Security Monitoring — The organisation monitors the security status of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) to detect security events indicative of a security incident.
desc.C1.a: Sources and Tools for Logging and Monitoring — The data sources and tools you include in logging and monitoring allow timely identification of events that might adversely affect security or resiliency of systems supporting essential function(s).
desc.C1.b: Securing Logs — You hold log data securely and grant appropriate access only to accounts with a business need. Log data is held for a suitable retention period.
desc.C1.c: Generating Alerts — Evidence of potential security incidents in your monitoring data is reliably identified and where appropriate triggers alerts.
desc.C1.d: Triage of Security Alerts — You contextualise alerts with knowledge of the threat and your systems, to identify security incidents as well as responding to all alerts appropriately.
desc.C1.e: Personnel Skills for Monitoring and Detection — Monitoring and detection personnel skills and roles (including outsourced) reflect governance and reporting requirements, expected threats and complexities of network/system data.
desc.C1.f: Understanding User & System Behaviour, and Threat Intelligence — Threats to operations of network and information systems and corresponding user/system behaviour are sufficiently understood. Used to detect cyber security incidents.
desc.C2: Threat Hunting — The organisation proactively seeks to detect adverse activity within networks and information systems even when the activity evades standard security solutions.
desc.C2.a: Threat Hunting — You proactively seek to detect adverse activity affecting (or with potential to affect) essential function(s) even when the activity evades standard prevent/detect solutions.
desc.D1: Response and Recovery Planning — There are well-defined and tested incident management processes in place that aim to ensure continuity of essential function(s) in the event of system or service failure. Mitigation activities to contain or limit the impact of compromise are also in place.
desc.D1.a: Response Plan — You have an up-to-date incident response plan grounded in a thorough risk assessment that takes account of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) and covers a range of incident scenarios.
desc.D1.b: Response and Recovery Capability — You have the capability to enact your incident response plan, including effective limitation of impact on essential function(s). During an incident, you have access to timely information on which to base response decisions.
desc.D1.c: Testing and Exercising — Your organisation carries out exercises to test response plans, using past incidents and scenarios drawn from threat intelligence and risk assessment.
desc.D2: Lessons Learned — When an incident occurs, steps are taken to understand its causes and to ensure remediating action is taken to protect against future incidents.
desc.D2.a: Post Incident Analysis — When an incident occurs, your organisation takes steps to understand its causes, informing appropriate remediating action.
desc.D2.b: Using Incidents to Drive Improvements — Your organisation uses lessons learned from incidents to improve security measures.

about.title: About the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework
about.blurb: A systematic, outcome-focused tool for assessing how well cyber risks to essential functions are managed. Used for self-assessment or by independent / regulatory assessors.

sections.h: A tool for assessing cyber resilience
p: The Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) provides a systematic and comprehensive approach to assessing the extent to which cyber risks to essential function(s) are being managed by the organisation responsible.

CAF-based assessments can be carried out either by the responsible organisation itself (self-assessment) or by an independent external entity, possibly a regulator / cyber oversight body or a suitably qualified organisation acting on behalf of a regulator, such as an NCSC assured commercial service provider.

The 4 high-level objectives and 14 principles are written in terms of outcomes — what needs to be achieved, rather than a checklist of what needs to be done. The CAF adds further detail through structured sets of Indicators of Good Practice (IGPs).

NCSC developed the CAF in its role as national technical authority for cyber security; NCSC itself has no regulatory responsibilities. Organisations subject to cyber regulation should consult their regulators on whether CAF should be used in the context of meeting regulatory requirements.

sections.intro: The CAF was developed to meet eight requirements:
l: Provide a suitable framework to assist in carrying out cyber resilience assessments.
Maintain the outcome-focused approach of the NCSC cyber security and resilience principles and discourage tick-box assessments.
Be compatible with appropriate existing cyber security guidance and standards.
Enable the identification of effective cyber security and resilience improvement activities.
Exist in a common core version which is sector-agnostic.
Be extensible to accommodate sector-specific elements as may be required.
Enable the setting of meaningful target security levels — possibly reflecting a regulator view of appropriate and proportionate security.
Be as straightforward and cost-effective to apply as possible.

p: Each top-level NCSC security and resilience principle defines a broad cyber security outcome. The precise approach to achieving it is not specified — it varies according to organisational circumstances.
Each principle breaks down into a collection of lower-level contributing outcomes, all of which will normally need to be achieved to fully satisfy the top-level principle.

Each contributing outcome is associated with a set of Indicators of Good Practice (IGPs). The IGPs describe the circumstances under which the outcome is judged ‘achieved’, ‘not achieved’, or (in some cases) ‘partially achieved’.

Assessment of contributing outcomes is primarily a matter of expert judgement. IGPs do not remove the requirement for informed use of cyber security expertise and sector knowledge — they are starting points, used flexibly alongside the NCSC top-level guidance.
Achieved (GREEN) — typical characteristics of an organisation fully achieving the outcome. All indicators would normally need to be present.
Not achieved (RED) — typical characteristics of an organisation not achieving the outcome. The presence of any one indicator is normally sufficient to justify a ‘not achieved’ assessment.

Partially achieved (AMBER) — when present, typical characteristics of an organisation partially achieving the outcome. Partial achievement should represent more than giving credit for doing something vaguely relevant.

head: IGPs are…
IGPs are not…
rows: Intended to help inform expert judgement.
A checklist to be used in an inflexible assessment process.
Important examples of what an assessor will normally need to consider — which may need to be supplemented in some cases.
An exhaustive list covering everything an assessor needs to consider.
Designed to be widely applicable across different organisations, but applicability needs to be established.
Guaranteed to apply verbatim to all organisations.

sections.h: Setting target levels and CAF profiles
p: Applying the CAF produces 41 individual assessments — one per contributing outcome. A result in which all 41 are assessed as ‘achieved’ indicates a level of cyber security some way beyond the bare minimum ‘basic cyber hygiene’ level.

A cyber oversight body sets target levels for organisations within their sector. One approach is to relate target levels to the ability to withstand specified categories of cyber attacks (basic capability, moderate capability, etc.) using the idea of CAF profiles.

A CAF profile consists of a mixture: some contributing outcomes to be met at ‘achieved’, some at ‘partially achieved’, and possibly some identified as ‘not applicable’ where the capability is not appropriate at the level of the profile.
It is not the responsibility of NCSC to mandate what represents appropriate and proportionate cyber security and resilience — any target is for the relevant cyber oversight body to define.

The common core of the CAF (objectives, principles, contributing outcomes and IGPs) is sector-agnostic — designed to be generally applicable to all organisations responsible for essential functions across all key sectors. Sector-specific aspects can include:
l: Sector-specific CAF profiles — target profiles defined by the relevant cyber oversight body, possibly from a regulatory perspective.
Sector-specific interpretations of contributing outcomes / IGPs — to better clarify meaning within a sector.
Sector-specific additional contributing outcomes / IGPs — where generic outcomes cannot adequately cover sector-specific cyber security requirements.

objectives.name: Managing Security Risk
objectives.desc: Appropriate organisational structures, policies, processes and procedures in place to understand, assess and systematically manage security risks to network and information systems supporting essential functions.

principles.name: Governance
principles.desc: The organisation has appropriate management policies, processes and procedures in place to govern its approach to the security of network and information systems.

outcomes.name: Board Direction
outcomes.desc: You have effective organisational security management led at board level and articulated clearly in corresponding policies.
achieved: Your organisation's approach and policy relating to the security of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) are owned and managed at board-level, communicated meaningfully to risk management decision-makers across the organisation.
Regular board-level discussions on security take place, based on timely and accurate information and informed by expert guidance.
There is a board-level individual with overall accountability for the security of network and information systems who drives regular discussion at board-level.
Board-level direction is translated into effective organisational practices that direct and control security of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).

The board has the information and understanding needed to effectively discuss how the security and resilience of network and information systems contributes to the delivery of essential function(s) and the potential impact from compromise.
Security is recognised as an important enabler for the resilience of essential function(s) and considered in all relevant discussions.
evidence: Information Security Policy approved by board (with version & sign-off date)
Board / executive committee minutes covering security topics
Board reporting pack with security KPIs and risk dashboard

outcomes.name: Roles and Responsibilities
outcomes.desc: Your organisation has established roles and responsibilities for the security of network and information systems at all levels, with clear and well-understood channels for communicating and escalating risks.

evidence: Security RACI matrix or accountability map
Job descriptions / role profiles for security roles (CISO, security manager, asset owners)

outcomes.name: Decision-making

achieved: Senior management have visibility of key risk decisions made throughout the organisation.

principles.name: Risk Management
principles.desc: The organisation takes appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand security risks to network and information systems supporting the operation of essential functions. This includes an overall organisational approach to risk management.

outcomes.name: Risk Management Process
outcomes.desc: Your organisation has effective internal processes for managing risks to the security and resilience of network and information systems related to essential function(s) and communicating associated activities.
achieved: Your organisational process ensures that security risks to network and information systems relevant to essential function(s) are identified, analysed, prioritised and managed.
Your approach to risk is focused on the possibility of adverse impact to essential function(s), leading to a detailed understanding of how impact might arise from possible threat actor actions.

Risk assessments are based on a clearly understood set of threat assumptions, informed by an up-to-date understanding of threats to essential function(s), your sector and wider national infrastructure.
Risk assessments are informed by an understanding of vulnerabilities in network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
The output of risk management is a clear set of traceable and prioritised security requirements that address risks in line with your organisational approach to security.
Significant conclusions reached are communicated to key security decision-makers and accountable individuals.
Risk assessments are dynamic and readily updated in light of relevant changes (technical changes, change of use, emergent technologies, new threat information).
The effectiveness of your risk management process is reviewed regularly and improvements made as required.
You anticipate technological developments that could be used to adversely impact network and information systems supporting essential function(s).

Risk Treatment Plan (RTP) tied to controls
Threat assumptions document supporting risk assessments
Records of risk assessment reviews after major changes (system, threat, regulation)

outcomes.name: Understanding Threat
outcomes.desc: You understand the capabilities, methods and techniques of threat actors and what network and information systems they may compromise to adversely impact essential function(s). This information is used to inform security and resilience risk management decisions.
achieved: You perform detailed threat analysis and understand how this applies to network and information systems supporting essential function(s) in the context of your sector and wider national infrastructure.
Your detailed understanding of threat includes the methods and techniques available to capable and well-resourced threat actors and how they could be used systematically against your systems.
You use appropriate techniques (e.g. attacker-perspective analysis) to anticipate probable attack methods, targets and objectives, and develop plausible scenarios.
You understand the different steps a capable threat actor would need to take to reach probable targets.
You identify and justify what measures can be used at each step to reduce the likelihood of the threat actor reaching probable targets or achieving their objectives.
You maintain a detailed understanding of current threats (e.g. by threat intelligence and proactive research).
You apply your detailed understanding of threat to inform risk management decision-making.
You have documented the steps required to undertake detailed threat analysis.
evidence: Threat intelligence subscriptions / feeds in use
Sector / national-infrastructure threat assessment reports
Threat-actor profile briefings (capability, methods, TTPs)
Attacker-perspective analysis (e.g. red-team report, attack-path analysis)
Documented detailed threat-analysis steps and how outputs inform decisions

outcomes.name: Assurance
outcomes.desc: You have gained confidence in the effectiveness of the security of your technology, people and processes relevant to the operation of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
achieved: You validate that the security measures protecting essential function(s) are effective and remain effective for the lifetime over which they are needed.
You understand the assurance methods available to you and choose appropriate methods to gain confidence in security.
Your confidence in the security as it relates to your technology, people and processes can be justified to, and verified by, a third party.

External assessment reports (CAF, ISO 27001, SOC 2, pen test)
Control-effectiveness testing evidence
Assurance methodology document
Tracker of assurance findings, prioritisation and remediation

principles.name: Asset Management
principles.desc: Everything required to deliver, maintain or support network and information systems necessary for essential functions is determined and understood. This includes data, people and systems, as well as supporting infrastructure (such as power or cooling).

outcomes.name: Asset Management
outcomes.desc: All assets required to deliver, maintain or support essential function(s) are determined, understood, prioritised and managed throughout their lifecycle.
achieved: All assets relevant to the secure operation of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) are identified and inventoried at suitable detail. The inventory is kept up-to-date.
Dependencies on supporting infrastructure (e.g. power, cooling) are recognised and recorded.
You have prioritised your assets according to their importance to the operation of essential function(s).
You have assigned responsibility for managing all assets, including physical assets, relevant to the operation of essential function(s).
Assets are managed with cyber security in mind throughout their lifecycle, from creation through to eventual decommissioning or disposal.

Asset classification and prioritisation matrix
Assigned asset owners (named individuals)
Dependency map including supporting infrastructure (power, cooling, comms)
Lifecycle policy covering creation through decommissioning / sanitisation

principles.name: Supply Chain

outcomes.name: Supply Chain
outcomes.desc: You understand and effectively manage the risks associated with suppliers to the security of network and information systems supporting essential function(s).
achieved: You have a deep understanding of your supply chain, including sub-contractors, and the wider risks it faces.

Your supply chain risk management considers risks from supply chain subversion by capable and well-resourced threat actors.
Critical suppliers can demonstrate appropriate and proportionate cyber security in the context of capable threat actors.
You have confidence that information held by suppliers essential to the operation of essential function(s) is appropriately protected.
You understand which contracts are relevant and include appropriate security obligations.
You have a proactive contract management approach (may include a contract management plan).
Customer/supplier ownership of responsibilities is defined in contracts.
All network connections and data sharing with third parties are managed effectively and proportionately.
Where appropriate, your incident management process and that of suppliers provide mutual support in incident resolution.
evidence: Supplier register with criticality ratings and sub-contractor visibility
Sample contracts showing security obligations and customer/supplier responsibility split
Supplier security assessment reports / due diligence records
Inventory of third-party network connections and data flows

outcomes.name: Secure Software Development and Support
outcomes.desc: You actively maximise the use of secure and supported software, whether developed internally or sourced externally, within network and information systems supporting essential function(s).

You consider the security of environments (development, test, production) including source code and repositories appropriate within the context of capable and well-resourced threat actors.

objectives.name: Protecting Against Cyber Attack
objectives.desc: Proportionate security measures are in place to protect network and information systems supporting essential functions from cyber attack.

Policies, processes and procedures are practical, usable and appropriate to mitigate risk of adverse impact to essential function(s).
Policies, processes and procedures that rely on user behaviour are practical, appropriate and achievable.
You review and update policies, processes and procedures at suitably regular intervals (and after major incidents).
Any changes to essential function(s) or threat triggers a review of policies, processes and procedures.

Policy review schedule and review records
Sample policies (acceptable use, access control, incident response, etc.)

principles.name: System Security

Personnel follow policies addressing all governance reporting requirements.
Personnel are empowered to look beyond fixed processes to investigate non-standard threats.
Personnel are aware of network and information systems and essential function(s), related assets, and can identify and prioritise alerts.
Personnel drive and shape new log data collection.
Personnel are capable of following all required workflows.
Personnel have sufficient understanding of operational context to enhance security monitoring.
Personnel deal with workload and cases effectively while identifying improvement areas.
evidence: Job descriptions / skills matrix for monitoring & detection personnel
Training records for monitoring staff
Outsourced provider SLA and skill assurance evidence
Workload metrics (alerts/analyst, time-to-triage)
Evidence personnel are empowered to investigate non-standard threats

outcomes.name: Understanding User & System Behaviour, and Threat Intelligence
outcomes.desc: Threats to operations of network and information systems and corresponding user/system behaviour are sufficiently understood. Used to detect cyber security incidents.
achieved: You track effectiveness of threat intelligence and actively share feedback with the threat community.
Threat intelligence feeds are selected using risk-based and threat-informed decisions based on business needs and sector.
You make relevant, reliable and actionable threat intelligence available to necessary users and systems promptly.
You contextualise threat intelligence and link it to why/how attacks take place.
You understand normal user and system abnormalities fully (you understand which systems should and should not communicate, and when).
Abnormalities monitored are based on the nature of adverse activities likely to impact essential function(s).
Abnormalities indicative of adverse activity are regularly updated to reflect changes in systems and current threat intelligence.
You can share threat intelligence (effective ways to detect adversaries) with the threat/defender community when required.
evidence: Threat intelligence subscriptions / feed selection rationale
Threat-intel community participation (sector, ISAC, government)
Behaviour baselining documentation per system / user role
Records of TI being made actionable in detections
Outbound threat-intel sharing evidence (when permitted)

principles.name: Threat Hunting
principles.desc: The organisation proactively seeks to detect adverse activity within networks and information systems even when the activity evades standard security solutions.

outcomes.name: Threat Hunting
outcomes.desc: You proactively seek to detect adverse activity affecting (or with potential to affect) essential function(s) even when the activity evades standard prevent/detect solutions.
achieved: You understand resources required for threat hunting and deploy them as part of business as usual.
You deploy threat hunting at a frequency matching risks posed to essential function(s).
Threat hunts follow pre-determined and documented methods (hypothesis-driven, data-driven, entity-driven) to identify adverse activity not detected by automation.
You turn threat hunts into automated detections and alerting where appropriate.
You routinely record details of threat hunts and post-hunt activities to drive improvements.
You have justified confidence in the effectiveness of threat hunts; the process is reviewed and updated to match risk.
You leverage automation to improve threat hunts (some stages automated).
Threat hunts focus on TTPs of threats over atomic IoCs (hashes, IPs, domains).
evidence: Threat hunting methodology (hypothesis / data / entity-driven)
Threat hunt records / reports with findings
Hunt-to-detection automation evidence
TTP-based hunt examples mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
Threat hunting frequency and resource plan

objectives.name: Minimising the Impact of Cyber Security Incidents
objectives.desc: Capabilities exist to minimise the adverse impact of a cyber security incident on the operation of essential functions, including their restoration where necessary.

principles.name: Response and Recovery Planning
principles.desc: There are well-defined and tested incident management processes in place that aim to ensure continuity of essential function(s) in the event of system or service failure. Mitigation activities to contain or limit the impact of compromise are also in place.

outcomes.name: Response Plan
outcomes.desc: You have an up-to-date incident response plan grounded in a thorough risk assessment that takes account of network and information systems supporting essential function(s) and covers a range of incident scenarios.
achieved: The incident response plan is based on clear understanding of security risks to systems supporting essential function(s).
The plan is comprehensive (covers complete incident lifecycle, roles, responsibilities, reporting) and covers known attack patterns and possible previously-unseen attacks.
The plan is documented and integrated with wider organisational business and supply chain plans, plus dependencies on supporting infrastructure.
The plan is communicated and understood by business areas involved with essential function(s).
evidence: Incident Response Plan covering full lifecycle
Risk-based scenario coverage (known and unseen attack patterns)
Stakeholder map (internal, supply chain, regulator, NCSC)
Plan version control and approval history
Plan accessible during IT outage (offline copies)

outcomes.name: Response and Recovery Capability
outcomes.desc: You have the capability to enact your incident response plan, including effective limitation of impact on essential function(s). During an incident, you have access to timely information on which to base response decisions.
achieved: You understand resources likely needed for response activities and have arrangements to make them available.
You understand information types needed to inform response decisions and have arrangements to make information available.
Response team members have skills, knowledge and authority to decide on response actions and carry them out.
Key roles are duplicated; operational delivery knowledge is shared.
Back-up mechanisms can be readily activated to allow continued (possibly reduced) operation of essential function(s) if primary systems fail.
Arrangements exist to augment incident response capabilities with external support if necessary.
evidence: Incident response team roster with skills and authority
Tooling inventory (forensics, comms, evidence handling)
External support arrangements (CSIRT retainer, regulator hotline)
Backup / reduced-mode operating procedures
Information sources available during an incident (asset, contact, dependency data)

outcomes.name: Testing and Exercising
outcomes.desc: Your organisation carries out exercises to test response plans, using past incidents and scenarios drawn from threat intelligence and risk assessment.
achieved: Exercise scenarios are based on incidents experienced by you and others, or composed using experience or threat intelligence.
Exercise scenarios are documented, regularly reviewed and validated.
Exercises are routinely run; findings are documented and used to refine response plans and protective security.
Exercises test all parts of your response cycle relating to essential function(s) (e.g. restoration of normal function levels).
evidence: Exercise plan / annual schedule
Documented exercise scenarios drawn from threat intel and past incidents
After-action reports from exercises
Coverage matrix showing all parts of response cycle tested
Lessons-learned actions tracked from each exercise

principles.name: Lessons Learned
principles.desc: When an incident occurs, steps are taken to understand its causes and to ensure remediating action is taken to protect against future incidents.

outcomes.name: Post Incident Analysis
outcomes.desc: When an incident occurs, your organisation takes steps to understand its causes, informing appropriate remediating action.
achieved: Post incident analysis is conducted routinely as a key part of lessons learned activities following an incident.
Post incident analysis is comprehensive: organisational factors (policies, processes), technical factors (system design, vulnerabilities), human factors (training, culture) and any threat changes.
All relevant incident data is made available to the analysis team.
Analysis considers what could have happened under plausible alternative circumstances ('what if'/'if only').
evidence: Post-incident review process / template
Sample post-incident review reports
Root-cause analysis records (technical, organisational, human factors)
'What if' / 'if only' alternative scenario analysis
Evidence that all relevant incident data is provided to analysts

outcomes.name: Using Incidents to Drive Improvements
outcomes.desc: Your organisation uses lessons learned from incidents to improve security measures.
achieved: You have a documented incident review process/policy ensuring lessons learned from each incident (including near misses) are identified, captured and acted upon.
Lessons learned cover reporting, roles, governance, skills and policies as well as technical aspects.
You use lessons learned to improve security measures, including updating and retesting response plans.
Security improvements identified from lessons learned are prioritised; highest priority improvements completed promptly.
Analysis is fed to senior management and incorporated into risk management and continuous improvement.
Your organisation maximises lessons by using 'what if'/'if only' scenario analysis.
Your organisation learns from reported incidents in your sector and the wider national infrastructure.
evidence: Lessons-learned register linked to incidents and near-misses
Improvement action tracker with priorities and completion dates
Sector / national-infrastructure incident-learning records
Continuous improvement reporting to senior management
Evidence of plan / control updates resulting from lessons learned
